title: Writing an LLM from scratch, part 16 -- layer normalisation
summary: Working through layer normalisation -- why do we do it, how does it work, and why doesn't it break everything?
markdown:
I'm now working through chapter 4 of [Sebastian Raschka](https://sebastianraschka.com/)'s book "[Build a Large Language Model (from Scratch)](https://www.manning.com/books/build-a-large-language-model-from-scratch)". It's the chapter where we put together the pieces that we've covered so far and wind up with a fully-trainable LLM, so there's a lot in there -- nothing quite as daunting as fully trainable self-attention was, but still stuff that needs thought.

Last time around I covered something that for me seemed absurdly simplistic for what it did -- the step that [converts the context vectors our attention layers come up with into output logits](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2025/05/llm-from-scratch-15-from-context-vectors-to-logits). Grasping how a single matrix multiplication could possibly do that took a bit of thought, but it was all clear in the end.

This time, layer normalisation.

### Why do we need it?

Looking at my mental model of an LLM at this point, it works like this:

-   We tokenise our input and convert the tokens into token embeddings and position embeddings, and then combine those for our input embeddings.
-   Those input embeddings are fed into a multi-head attention layer, which spits out context vectors -- a kind of representation of what each token means in the context of the other tokens to its left.
-   Those context vectors are fed into a second MHA layer, which does the same but at "a higher level" -- kind of like the way that each successive layer in a vision NN like a CNN has a higher level of abstraction: the first layer detects edges, the next corners, and so on up to the *n*th layer that can detect dogs' faces (though of course the abstractions the LLM is building are unlikely to be as human-comprehensible as those).
-   After a number of layers, we have context vectors for each token that, in embedding space, point in the direction of the most probable next one, given the token itself and the ones to its left.
-   We run those final context vectors through a single unbiased linear layer with no activation function -- a simple matrix multiplication -- to project them from embedding space to vocab space, which gives us our logits.

That actually feels like a pretty complete system, and I rather suspect that in principle, an LLM might work just with those calculations. [1](#fn-1)

But -- as I said in the last post -- the code in the book is "folding, spindling and mutilating" the context vectors. Each attention layer isn't just the [pure attention mechanism](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2025/03/llm-from-scratch-8-trainable-self-attention), made [causal](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2025/03/llm-from-scratch-9-causal-attention), with [dropout](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2025/03/llm-from-scratch-10-dropout) and [run multiple times in parallel](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2025/04/llm-from-scratch-12-multi-head-attention). A few other things are happening on top of that.

As far as I understand it, these extra steps are to make them trainable in the real world. My naive description above, without those steps, might work in principle, but if you actually tried to train a model that worked that way, you'd not get great results.

Layer normalisation is one of the tricks used to make the LLM trainable, and I think it's pretty easy to understand, at least at a basic level.

### What is it?

Imagine we have a matrix of context vectors that came out of our multi-head attention module. Disregarding batches, it's an n×demb matrix -- one row for each of our n tokens in the input, each row being an embedding vector of length demb.

For layer normalisation, what we do is essentially go through each row, and for each one adjust the numbers so that it has a mean of 0, and a variance of 1. The mean is (of course) the sum of all the numbers in the vector divided by its length, and the variance is a measure of how much the numbers differ from the mean (more about that later).

So, what we're doing is a kind of normalisation of the "sizes" of the vectors in a rather abstract sense.

My mental model for this maps it to the way a producer would normalise analog audio signals going into a mixing desk.

Analog signals are messy -- for example, the voltage from a microphone might have a DC bias, which means that instead of oscillating around 0 volts, it could oscillate around 3V or something. Different input signals might have different DC biases, so you would want to fix that first so that you can mix them. Likewise, different signals might be at different levels -- an active microphone might have a much higher voltage than a a passive one, and a direct feed from a synth might be at another different level.

So you'd want to eliminate that DC bias (which maps to setting the mean to zero), and get them all to roughly the same level -- line level (mapping to making the variance one). Once you have that done, you can then set the levels appropriately for the mix (which would involve making some louder, some quieter, and so on -- but at least you're starting from a point where they're consistent).

It's not an exact match for what normalisation is doing -- in particular the line level part -- but I've found it useful.

### Why?

Raschka explains that normalisation is required to avoid problems like exploding or vanishing gradients. I think that's worth going through.

I'll assume that you already know how gradient descent works, but it's worth writing a quick overview just to set the stage.

When we're training something with gradient descent, we run some inputs through it and then measure the *error* -- how far off the result was from what we wanted. If we simplify a bit, for our LLM, if we feed in:

```
the fat cat sat on the
```

...and we want `mat` to be the predicted next token, then we create an error function that will be zero if that is what the LLM comes up with, and a number larger than zero if it predicts `dog` or whatever. (I think that the details of how we write an error function that does this effectively will come in the next chapter. Please also note that I'm grossly simplifying here -- as I covered in the last post, we're actually predicting next tokens for every token in the input rather than just the last one. But that doesn't matter for this bit.)

We then use differentiation to work out, for every parameter, what the gradient is against that error. That means, essentially, what direction would we move it in, and how much, if we wanted to make the error one unit higher. We want to make the error lower rather than higher, of course -- and we don't want to make it exactly one unit lower, we only want to move a small distance in the "error lower" direction. So we multiply the gradient by our learning rate (a number less than one), then subtract it from the parameter so that we move a small distance in the right direction.

Once that has been done for all parameters, we can run another training sample through and repeat until we're done.

The nice thing about libraries like PyTorch is that they abstract away all of the differentiation to work out these gradients completely, and we don't need to do any of the maths ourselves. But, unfortunately, it's a kind of leaky abstraction -- that is, we can't completely forget about what is going on under the hood.

With a multi-layer network like an LLM, the way the gradient calculation works is that it firstly calculates the gradients for the parameters in the last layer -- the ones that directly produced the output we're trying to correct. These gradients are then used as part of the calculations for the penultimate layer, and so on -- back-propagation of the error from the "end" of the network to the start.

So, let's think about vanishing and exploding gradients. These are problems that affect the early layers in the network -- the ones that are processed later during backprop. The gradients that you have for the layers at the "end" of the network are pretty solid, but as they're propagated back to earlier ones, they're multiplied by various numbers -- the parameters themselves, for example -- and as a result, they (of course) get larger or smaller.

It's entirely possible for a particular gradient, as it heads backwards, to approach or become zero. That means it kind of reaches a dead end -- it can't have any effect on the layer where it reaches zero, or on any of the earlier ones. Hence, vanishing gradient.

An exploding gradient is (fairly obviously) the opposite issue -- a gradient gets multiplied by a large number, or a series of large numbers, and becomes so large that it drowns out all of the others.

> Remember that when a gradient propagates back from layer n to layer n−1, all of the gradients in layer n−1 will depend on all of the gradients in n, assuming that the network is fully connected between layers. So that means that one huge gradient in layer n will have an oversized effect on all of the gradients in n−1.

So, the point of this layer normalisation is to stop that from happening; to stop our gradients from either vanishing or exploding as they propagate back from the last layer to first.

To use the analog audio signal metaphor from earlier -- we're trying to set things up so that the guitar isn't so loud that we can't even hear the drums, and so that the singer is at least audible enough that we can can hear when she's singing.

### How?

So, how do we set the mean to zero and the variance to one for each token's context vector?

#### The mean

The mean is really easy: we simply work out the existing mean of the vector, and then subtract that from all of the values with a broadcast subtraction. That pretty obviously sets the mean to zero. For example, if we start with the vector (2,4,6):

-   The mean is:
    
    2+4+63\=123\=4
-   Subtracting the mean from each of those gives us
    
    (2−44−46−4)\=(−202)
-   ...and the mean of *that* is:
    
    −2+0+23\=03\=0

#### The variance

To make the variance equal to one, we work out the existing variance, and then divide by its square root (the standard deviation). My initial reaction was "why not divide by the variance itself?".

To answer that, I think it's worth doing a bit of a refresher on how variance and standard deviation work.

To calculate variance, you work out the mean of a vector, then calculate for each element the difference between the element and the mean, then square all of those, then take the average of that. [2](#fn-2)

So, for the vector (2,4,6); we already know from above that the differences from the mean are (−2,0,2).

-   Squaring those gives us:
    
    (−22,02,22)\=(4,0,4)
-   We now work out the mean of that:
    
    4+0+43\=83\=2.6˙

That's the variance, and the square root of that is called the standard deviation. The squaring is necessary because we want to make the numbers positive -- exactly why we do that rather than using the absolute value is something I'm sure I was taught sometime in the late 80s, but I won't dig into it now. [3](#fn-3) (I'm considering a separate blog post series, something like "high school maths refreshed for older devs digging into machine learning". If you'd be interested, please leave a comment below!)

So, why do we divide by the standard deviation rather than the variance itself?

Let's think about what dividing by the standard deviation does. It essentially converts each element in the vector into a number that says how many standard deviations it is away from the mean. So if something is one standard deviation away from the mean in the original vector, it will have the value 1 if it's one SD greater than the mean, or −1 if it's one SD less that the mean.

It's pretty clear that the standard deviation of such a vector will be one, almost by definition! We've scaled all of the numbers such that the numbers that were one SD from the mean are 1 or −1, but those numbers are still the ones that are one SD away from the mean, so the SD must therefore be one.

And because the variance is the SD squared, that means that it must also be one.

Now imagine that we divided by the variance. That would mean that each element would be a measure of how many variances its "original" was away from the mean. Assuming that the variance was not already one, it must be a number either smaller or larger than one. That means that the numbers one SD away from the mean must now be something that is not one, So the SD is no longer one and neither is its square, the variance.

Another way to look at it is in terms of units. Let's say that we were dealing with a vector where each number was a measurement of a length in meters. What we're trying to do is convert it to a vector that is normalised such that each number is unitless.

Our variance was calculated by working out the mean (an average of measurements in meters, so it must be in meters), then subtracting that from each measurement (so we have a list of measurements' offsets from their mean -- also meters), and then we square those, getting a list of numbers that -- unit-wise -- represent square meters. We then divide them by the length of the vector (which is unitless).

So the variance, if we consider it in terms of its units, is in square meters, If we were to divide the list of measurements by that number, we'd get values that represented some kind of *something* per meter -- that is, the unit would be m−1.

But what we want to do is simply turn those measurements into dimensionless values. That means that we need to divide by something that has units of meters -- which is the standard deviation.

I'm not 100% happy with those explanations -- the latter, in particular, like all units-based explanations, is susceptible to issues with unitless values. For example, there could be a multiplication by some constant in there, or we might use the length of the vector squared.

However, I think they're enough for now.

### But doesn't this break our embeddings?

Having understood how the normalisation works, there was one remaining problem I had in my mental model -- something that applies to all of the manipulations that we apply to the output of the multi-head attention mechanism, but that is particularly clear here.

Embedding vectors represent meaning; in general, the length isn't super-important for that, but the direction is. So if we change the direction of an embedding, we change its meaning -- and that sounds bad.

Scaling a context vector by its standard deviation just changes the vector's length, so that's not super-important. But changing its mean changes the direction!

For example, consider this toy embedding in a 2D space, (1,5). Let's chart it:

![A chart of the vector (1, 5)](https://www.gilesthomas.com/post-assets/layer-normalisation/vector-1-5.svg "A chart of the vector (1, 5)")

We set the mean to zero by working out the mean of the original numbers:

1+52\=62\=3

...then subtracting that mean from each of them:

(1−35−3)\=(−22)

We don't really need to chart that to see that it's not pointing in the same direction as the original, but let's do it anyway:

![A chart of the vector (-2, 2)](https://www.gilesthomas.com/post-assets/layer-normalisation/vector--2-2.svg "A chart of the vector (-2, 2)")

The division of this vector by its standard deviation would just shrink it, so that's not an issue -- remember that the length of an embedding vector isn't really important -- but the complete change in direction felt like it would be an issue.

My concern was that we had these context vectors coming out of our multi-head attention layers that had some kind of meaning. Setting the mean to zero in this normalisation layer looked like it was going to completely break them!

The mistake I was making was in thinking that the context vectors coming out of the MHA layer were meaningful vectors in embedding space. When we train our LLM, we're training it as a whole -- indeed, there's no real guarantee that the context vectors moving between attention layers have any real meaning at all. The only constraint we're applying (via our error function and gradient descent via backprop) is that the context vectors from the very last layer point in the direction of the predicted next token's embedding.

Now, it's reasonable to assume that the context vectors that are passed between the layers have some kind of meaning in embedding space -- given how people talk about them, I imagine some tests have been done to check, though perhaps that's a deep interpretability problem -- but the important thing is that what is passed between the layers has already gone through this normalisation.

That is, if we assume that what is coming out of a single layer -- MHA, normalisation, and all of the other stuff we're going to cover in the next few posts -- is a meaningful context vector in embedding space, then the weights that we have inside the MHA layer itself -- our Wquery, Wkey, and Wvalue matrices -- will be trained so that the values that come out of that pure MHA part of the layer will not be in embedding space in and of themselves. They will instead be trained to output numbers that *will* be in embedding space, *after they have been normalised*.

The model I'm forming here is that the normalisation is not so much a mechanical thing that we're doing to the numbers that flow through the network; it's more of a constraint on the kinds of values that can flow through at particular points, and during training, our network learns to shape the "unconstrained" parts -- the attention weights -- so that as a whole it does the desired task while working within those constraints.

A work-in-progress metaphor I have for this is that it's kind of like a company where the interactions between teams are strongly codified, but teams can work pretty much independently so long as they present the required "API" to other teams. I've heard that AWS works kind of like this; the team that is responsible for -- say -- their email-sending service has a lot of freedom in *how* they work, so long as they provide an email service that operates in a particular way.

Might need more work, but I'll see if it sticks :-)

### Scale and shift

Once we've done all of this and have our context vectors all nicely aligned with a mean of 0 and a variance of 1, there's one final step; we multiply them by a *scale* vector, then add on a *shift* vector. Each of these has a length equal to the embedding dimensions -- that is, the zeroth number in a given context vector is multiplied by the zeroth one in the *scale* vector, then has the zeroth in the *shift* vector added on. These vectors are trainable -- a given normalisation step will use the same ones for every context vector, but the actual values to use will be one of the parameters learned as part of the training.

That kind of feels like it's undoing some of the work we've done to normalise things! I also can't think of an obvious mapping for either of them in the audio metaphor I've been using so far.

But at a stretch, perhaps the scale vector could be seen as some kind of equaliser step? What it's doing is is saying that after this normalisation step, we're going to increase how much the context vectors point in certain dimensions, and decrease it in others. Perhaps an engineering trick that just happens to work? That feels like a bit of a cop-out, though.

The shift vector is even harder to put into the audio metaphor. I was thinking that it might be to avoid issues with the activation function that comes up later (having set the mean to zero means that we might "throw away" a lot of information with an activation function that treats numbers less than zero as zero), but there's a linear layer before that, which could perfectly well handle that side of things.

After discussion with Claude, I think that the best way to look at it is that having a mean of zero and a variance of one is not necessarily the best set of statistical properties for the context vectors to have. By setting all of them to those values, but then applying scale and shift, we give the model a way to learn what the most appropriate statistical properties for them to have actually are, and then to use that.

The important thing is that all of the context vectors coming in will have different variances and means, while the ones going out will have the same. So perhaps that still works in the terms of "getting all of the incoming signals to the same level" metaphor, albeit at a level of abstraction that might be becoming a bit too high...

It's still a little foggy in my mind, though. Perhaps something where just doing some experiments would help -- another one to add to my ever-growing list of things to try out later!

### Wrapping up

So, as a first draft of a mental model for this -- layer normalisation constrains the values coming out of a particular attention layer so that they have a mean of zero -- no "DC bias" -- and they are within a reasonably similar range -- line signal level -- so that we don't have issues with exploding or vanishing gradients. We then apply a scale vector and a shift vector, which means that they now have the same mean and variance, but not necessarily zero and one.

That all seems pretty reasonable! I think we can wrap this one up here, and next time I'll move on to another part of the folding, spindling and mutilating that we do to the outputs of our simple multi-head attention modules in order to make the network trainable and able to do its job.

[Here's a link to the next post in this series](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2025/08/llm-from-scratch-17-the-feed-forward-network).

* * *

1.  I realised this isn't quite right while writing [the next post in the series](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2025/07/llm-from-scratch-17-the-feed-forward-network). [↩](#fnref-1)
    
2.  Raschka points out that there is an actually more common way of doing this that applies "Bessel's correction", where instead of taking the mean of the squared differences, you add them up and then divide by n−1, where n is the number of elements in the vector, instead of just dividing by n. PyTorch actually does that by default, but he has code to tell it not to. Obviously the difference between dividing by n or by n−1 becomes pretty minor as n gets big (like it is with the hundreds of embedding dimensions LLMs use) so it doesn't really change things much -- the code to not use it is for compatibility with the pre-generated GPT-2 weights that we load into the LLM later, which were trained without this correction.
    
    One thing that I noticed while messing around a bit with this is that whether or not we apply the correction doesn't change the procedure we need to follow; if we calculate the variance without the correction and then divide by the square root of that, we will get something that has a variance of 1 if that second variance is also calculated without the correction. Likewise, if we do both calculations with the correction applied, we'll also get a variance of 1. If we mix and match then we'll get weird results, but that would be a silly thing to do anyway. [↩](#fnref-2)
    
3.  When I ran this past ChatGPT as a pre-post review, it helpfully pointed out that squaring is differentiable, while the the absolute value is not at 0. This is a good point, because we need everything to be differentiable in order to do gradient descent. That said, it seems unlikely that that was the original reason when the concept was invented way back when, and of course ReLU is also not technically differentiable -- but there are workarounds. Worth noting, though. [↩](#fnref-3)

The mean is (of course) the sum of all the numbers in the vector divided by its length, and the variance is a measure of how much the numbers differ from the mean (more about that later). 层归一化本质上就是遍历每一行，并调整其中的数字，使该行的均值为 0、方差为 1。均值（当然）是向量中所有数字之和除以向量长度；方差则衡量这些数字偏离均值的程度（后面会详细讲）。 So, what we're doing is a kind of normalisation of the "sizes" of the vectors in a rather abstract sense. 所以，我们做的是一种相当抽象意义上的向量“大小”归一化。 My mental model for this maps it to the way a producer would normalise analog audio signals going into a mixing desk. 我对它的心智模型，是把它类比成制作人将输入调音台的模拟音频信号归一化的过程。 Analog signals are messy -- for example, the voltage from a microphone might have a DC bias, which means that instead of oscillating around 0 volts, it could oscillate around 3V or something. Different input signals might have different DC biases, so you would want to fix that first so that you can mix them. Likewise, different signals might be at different levels -- an active microphone might have a much higher voltage than a a passive one, and a direct feed from a synth might be at another different level. 模拟信号很杂乱——比如，麦克风电压可能带有直流偏置，也就是说它不是围绕 0 伏振荡，而是可能围绕 3V 之类的电压振荡。不同输入信号可能有不同的直流偏置，所以要先修正它们才能混音。同样，不同信号的电平也可能不同——主动式麦克风的电压可能比被动式高很多，合成器的直接馈送又可能处在另一个电平。 So you'd want to eliminate that DC bias (which maps to setting the mean to zero), and get them all to roughly the same level -- line level (mapping to making the variance one). Once you have that done, you can then set the levels appropriately for the mix (which would involve making some louder, some quieter, and so on -- but at least you're starting from a point where they're consistent). 因此，你会想消除直流偏置（对应于把均值设为零），并把它们调到大致相同的电平——线路电平（对应于让方差为一）。完成后，就可以为混音适当设置各路电平（有的调大、有的调小等等——但至少起点是一致的）。 It's not an exact match for what normalisation is doing -- in particular the line level part -- but I've found it useful. 这并不完全等同于归一化所做的事情——尤其是线路电平那一部分——但这个类比对我很有帮助。 ### Why? 为什么？ Raschka explains that normalisation is required to avoid problems like exploding or vanishing gradients. I think that's worth going through. Raschka 解释说，归一化是为了避免梯度爆炸或梯度消失之类的问题。我觉得值得把这件事走一遍。 I'll assume that you already know how gradient descent works, but it's worth writing a quick overview just to set the stage. 我假设你已经知道梯度下降如何工作，不过先快速回顾一下也有助于铺垫。 When we're training something with gradient descent, we run some inputs through it and then measure the *error* -- how far off the result was from what we wanted. If we simplify a bit, for our LLM, if we feed in: 用梯度下降训练某个东西时，我们把一些输入送进去，然后衡量*误差*——结果与期望相差多远。简单化一点，对我们的 LLM 来说，如果输入： ``` the fat cat sat on the ``` ...and we want `mat` to be the predicted next token, then we create an error function that will be zero if that is what the LLM comes up with, and a number larger than zero if it predicts `dog` or whatever. (I think that the details of how we write an error function that does this effectively will come in the next chapter. Please also note that I'm grossly simplifying here -- as I covered in the last post, we're actually predicting next tokens for every token in the input rather than just the last one. But that doesn't matter for this bit.) ……而我们希望 “mat” 成为预测的下一个词元，那么就创建一个误差函数：LLM 预测出它时误差为零，预测出 “dog” 或其他词时误差大于零。（我想，如何有效编写这种误差函数的细节会在下一章出现。还请注意，我这里做了极大的简化——正如上一篇文章所述，我们实际上会为输入中的每个词元预测下一个词元，而不只是最后一个。不过这对本段不重要。） We then use differentiation to work out, for every parameter, what the gradient is against that error. That means, essentially, what direction would we move it in, and how much, if we wanted to make the error one unit higher. We want to make the error lower rather than higher, of course -- and we don't want to make it exactly one unit lower, we only want to move a small distance in the "error lower" direction. So we multiply the gradient by our learning rate (a number less than one), then subtract it from the parameter so that we move a small distance in the right direction. 然后，我们用微分求出每个参数相对于该误差的梯度。也就是说，如果想让误差增加一个单位，我们会把参数朝哪个方向移动、移动多少。我们当然想让误差降低，而不是升高；也不想让它恰好降低一个单位，只需沿着“误差降低”的方向移动一小段距离。因此，将梯度乘以学习率（一个小于一的数），再从参数中减去结果，就会朝正确方向移动一小步。 Once that has been done for all parameters, we can run another training sample through and repeat until we're done. 对所有参数完成这一操作后，我们可以再输入一个训练样本并重复，直到结束。 The nice thing about libraries like PyTorch is that they abstract away all of the differentiation to work out these gradients completely, and we don't need to do any of the maths ourselves. But, unfortunately, it's a kind of leaky abstraction -- that is, we can't completely forget about what is going on under the hood. PyTorch 这类库的好处是，它们把求梯度所需的全部微分运算抽象掉了，我们不必亲自做数学计算。但遗憾的是，这是一种“泄漏的抽象”——也就是说，我们不能完全忘记底层发生了什么。 With a multi-layer network like an LLM, the way the gradient calculation works is that it firstly calculates the gradients for the parameters in the last layer -- the ones that directly produced the output we're trying to correct. These gradients are then used as part of the calculations for the penultimate layer, and so on -- back-propagation of the error from the "end" of the network to the start. 对于 LLM 这样的多层网络，梯度计算的方式是先计算最后一层参数的梯度——也就是直接产生待修正输出的那些参数。接着，这些梯度会参与倒数第二层的计算，如此继续——误差从网络“末端”反向传播到起点。 So, let's think about vanishing and exploding gradients. These are problems that affect the early layers in the network -- the ones that are processed later during backprop. The gradients that you have for the layers at the "end" of the network are pretty solid, but as they're propagated back to earlier ones, they're multiplied by various numbers -- the parameters themselves, for example -- and as a result, they (of course) get larger or smaller. 那么来想想梯度消失和梯度爆炸。这些问题会影响网络早期的层——它们在反向传播时较晚才处理。网络“末端”各层的梯度相当稳定，但向更早层传播时，会乘上各种数字——比如参数本身——所以自然会变大或变小。 It's entirely possible for a particular gradient, as it heads backwards, to approach or become zero. That means it kind of reaches a dead end -- it can't have any effect on the layer where it reaches zero, or on any of the earlier ones. Hence, vanishing gradient. 某个梯度在向后传播时完全可能趋近于零或变成零。这就像走进死胡同：它对到达零值的那一层以及更早的层都无法产生影响。因此叫作梯度消失。 An exploding gradient is (fairly obviously) the opposite issue -- a gradient gets multiplied by a large number, or a series of large numbers, and becomes so large that it drowns out all of the others. 梯度爆炸（很明显）则是相反的问题——梯度乘上一个很大的数，或一串很大的数，变得大到淹没其他所有梯度。 > Remember that when a gradient propagates back from layer n to layer n−1, all of the gradients in layer n−1 will depend on all of the gradients in n, assuming that the network is fully connected between layers. So that means that one huge gradient in layer n will have an oversized effect on all of the gradients in n−1. 记住，当梯度从第 n 层反向传播到第 n−1 层时，假设层间是全连接的，第 n−1 层的所有梯度都会依赖第 n 层的所有梯度。这意味着第 n 层中的一个巨大梯度会对第 n−1 层的全部梯度产生过大的影响。 So, the point of this layer normalisation is to stop that from happening; to stop our gradients from either vanishing or exploding as they propagate back from the last layer to first. 所以，层归一化的目的就是阻止这种情况；当梯度从最后一层传回第一层时，防止它们消失或爆炸。 To use the analog audio signal metaphor from earlier -- we're trying to set things up so that the guitar isn't so loud that we can't even hear the drums, and so that the singer is at least audible enough that we can can hear when she's singing. 沿用前面的模拟音频信号比喻——我们要把系统设置成：吉他不会响到鼓声完全听不见，歌手也至少足够响，让我们能听到她在唱歌。 ### How? 怎么做？ So, how do we set the mean to zero and the variance to one for each token's context vector? 那么，怎样让每个词元的上下文向量均值为零、方差为一呢？ #### The mean 均值 The mean is really easy: we simply work out the existing mean of the vector, and then subtract that from all of the values with a broadcast subtraction. That pretty obviously sets the mean to zero. For example, if we start with the vector (2,4,6): 均值很简单：先算出向量当前的均值，再用广播减法从所有值中减去它。这样显然会把均值设为零。例如，从向量 (2,4,6) 开始： - The mean is: 均值是： 2+4+63\=123\=4 - Subtracting the mean from each of those gives us 从每个数字中减去均值，得到： (2−44−46−4)\=(−202) - ...and the mean of *that* is: ……而这个结果的*均值*是： −2+0+23\=03\=0 #### The variance 方差 To make the variance equal to one, we work out the existing variance, and then divide by its square root (the standard deviation). My initial reaction was "why not divide by the variance itself?". 要让方差等于一，我们先算出当前方差，再除以它的平方根（标准差）。我最初的反应是：“为什么不直接除以方差本身？” To answer that, I think it's worth doing a bit of a refresher on how variance and standard deviation work. 要回答这个问题，我觉得有必要复习一下方差和标准差的工作方式。 To calculate variance, you work out the mean of a vector, then calculate for each element the difference between the element and the mean, then square all of those, then take the average of that. [2](#fn-2) 计算方差时，先求向量均值，再计算每个元素与均值的差，把所有差值平方，然后求这些平方值的平均数。[2](#fn-2) So, for the vector (2,4,6); we already know from above that the differences from the mean are (−2,0,2). 对于向量 (2,4,6)，我们已经知道它们与均值的差是 (−2,0,2)。 - Squaring those gives us: 把这些差值平方，得到： (−22,02,22)\=(4,0,4) - We now work out the mean of that: 现在求它们的均值： 4+0+43\=83\=2.6˙ That's the variance, and the square root of that is called the standard deviation. The squaring is necessary because we want to make the numbers positive -- exactly why we do that rather than using the absolute value is something I'm sure I was taught sometime in the late 80s, but I won't dig into it now. [3](#fn-3) (I'm considering a separate blog post series, something like "high school maths refreshed for older devs digging into machine learning". If you'd be interested, please leave a comment below!) 这就是方差，它的平方根称为标准差。必须平方是因为我们希望数字变成正数——至于为什么这样做而不是取绝对值，我肯定在 80 年代末某个时候学过，但这里就不深究了。[3](#fn-3)（我在考虑另写一个系列，比如“给钻研机器学习的年长开发者复习高中数学”。如果你感兴趣，请在下面留言！） So, why do we divide by the standard deviation rather than the variance itself? 那么，为什么除以标准差，而不是方差本身？ Let's think about what dividing by the standard deviation does. It essentially converts each element in the vector into a number that says how many standard deviations it is away from the mean. So if something is one standard deviation away from the mean in the original vector, it will have the value 1 if it's one SD greater than the mean, or −1 if it's one SD less that the mean. 想想除以标准差做了什么。它本质上把向量中的每个元素转换成一个数字，表示该元素距离均值有多少个标准差。如果原向量中某个元素距均值一个标准差，那么它比均值高一个标准差时值为 1，低一个标准差时值为 −1。 It's pretty clear that the standard deviation of such a vector will be one, almost by definition! We've scaled all of the numbers such that the numbers that were one SD from the mean are 1 or −1, but those numbers are still the ones that are one SD away from the mean, so the SD must therefore be one. 很明显，这样的向量标准差会是 1，几乎是定义如此！我们把所有数字缩放到：原来距均值一个标准差的数字变成 1 或 −1；但它们仍然是距均值一个标准差的数字，所以标准差必然为 1。 And because the variance is the SD squared, that means that it must also be one. 又因为方差是标准差的平方，所以方差也必然为 1。 Now imagine that we divided by the variance. That would mean that each element would be a measure of how many variances its "original" was away from the mean. Assuming that the variance was not already one, it must be a number either smaller or larger than one. That means that the numbers one SD away from the mean must now be something that is not one, So the SD is no longer one and neither is its square, the variance. 现在假设我们除以方差。这意味着每个元素表示其“原值”距离均值有多少个方差。假设方差原本不是一，它必然大于或小于一。这会使原来距均值一个标准差的数字变成不是一的值，于是标准差不再是一，平方后的方差也不再是一。 Another way to look at it is in terms of units. Let's say that we were dealing with a vector where each number was a measurement of a length in meters. What we're trying to do is convert it to a vector that is normalised such that each number is unitless. 换个角度，从单位来理解。假设向量中的每个数字都是以米为单位的长度测量值。我们想把它转换成一个归一化向量，使每个数字都无量纲。 Our variance was calculated by working out the mean (an average of measurements in meters, so it must be in meters), then subtracting that from each measurement (so we have a list of measurements' offsets from their mean -- also meters), and then we square those, getting a list of numbers that -- unit-wise -- represent square meters. We then divide them by the length of the vector (which is unitless). 计算方差时，我们先求均值（米制测量值的平均数，所以单位是米），然后从每个测量值中减去它（得到每个测量值相对于均值的偏移，同样是米），再把偏移平方，得到一串按单位计算代表平方米的数字。最后除以向量长度（无量纲）。 So the variance, if we consider it in terms of its units, is in square meters, If we were to divide the list of measurements by that number, we'd get values that represented some kind of *something* per meter -- that is, the unit would be m−1. 因此，从单位角度看，方差的单位是平方米。如果用这个数去除测量值列表，会得到某种*东西*每米的值——也就是单位 m−1。 But what we want to do is simply turn those measurements into dimensionless values. That means that we need to divide by something that has units of meters -- which is the standard deviation. 但我们真正想做的只是把这些测量值变成无量纲值。因此需要除以一个单位为米的量——也就是标准差。 I'm not 100% happy with those explanations -- the latter, in particular, like all units-based explanations, is susceptible to issues with unitless values. For example, there could be a multiplication by some constant in there, or we might use the length of the vector squared. 我对这些解释并不是百分之百满意——尤其是后一个，和所有基于单位的解释一样，容易受到无量纲值问题的影响。比如，表达式里可能有一个常数乘法，或者我们可能使用向量长度的平方。 However, I think they're enough for now. 不过，我认为现在这些解释已经够用了。 ### But doesn't this break our embeddings? 但这不会破坏我们的嵌入吗？ Having understood how the normalisation works, there was one remaining problem I had in my mental model -- something that applies to all of the manipulations that we apply to the output of the multi-head attention mechanism, but that is particularly clear here. 理解归一化的工作方式后，我的心智模型里还剩一个问题——它其实适用于我们对多头注意力机制输出所做的所有处理，只是在这里尤其明显。 Embedding vectors represent meaning; in general, the length isn't super-important for that, but the direction is. So if we change the direction of an embedding, we change its meaning -- and that sounds bad. 嵌入向量表示含义；一般来说，长度并不特别重要，方向才重要。因此，如果改变嵌入的方向，就会改变它的含义——听起来不妙。 Scaling a context vector by its standard deviation just changes the vector's length, so that's not super-important. But changing its mean changes the direction! 按标准差缩放上下文向量只会改变向量长度，所以不太重要——记住，嵌入向量的长度其实没那么重要。但改变均值会改变方向！ For example, consider this toy embedding in a 2D space, (1,5). Let's chart it: 例如，考虑二维空间中的玩具嵌入 (1,5)。我们画出来： ![A chart of the vector (1, 5)](https://www.gilesthomas.com/post-assets/layer-normalisation/vector-1-5.svg "A chart of the vector (1, 5)") We set the mean to zero by working out the mean of the original numbers: 我们先求原数字的均值，将均值设为零： 1+52\=62\=3 ...then subtracting that mean from each of them: ……然后从每个数字中减去这个均值： (1−35−3)\=(−22) We don't really need to chart that to see that it's not pointing in the same direction as the original, but let's do it anyway: 不用画图也能看出它没有指向原来的方向，不过我们还是画出来看看： ![A chart of the vector (-2, 2)](https://www.gilesthomas.com/post-assets/layer-normalisation/vector--2-2.svg "A chart of the vector (-2, 2)") The division of this vector by its standard deviation would just shrink it, so that's not an issue -- remember that the length of an embedding vector isn't really important -- but the complete change in direction felt like it would be an issue. 将该向量除以标准差只会让它缩短，所以不是问题——记住，嵌入向量的长度其实不重要——但方向完全改变，感觉就像是个问题。 My concern was that we had these context vectors coming out of our multi-head attention layers that had some kind of meaning. Setting the mean to zero in this normalisation layer looked like it was going to completely break them! 我担心的是，多头注意力层输出的这些上下文向量带有某种含义。这个归一化层把均值设为零，看起来会把它们彻底破坏！ The mistake I was making was in thinking that the context vectors coming out of the MHA layer were meaningful vectors in embedding space. When we train our LLM, we're training it as a whole -- indeed, there's no real guarantee that the context vectors moving between attention layers have any real meaning at all. The only constraint we're applying (via our error function and gradient descent via backprop) is that the context vectors from the very last layer point in the direction of the predicted next token's embedding. 我犯的错误，是把 MHA 层输出的上下文向量当成了嵌入空间中有意义的向量。训练 LLM 时，我们训练的是一个整体——事实上，注意力层之间流动的上下文向量根本不保证有任何真正的含义。我们施加的唯一约束（通过误差函数、梯度下降和反向传播）是：最后一层的上下文向量要指向预测的下一个词元的嵌入方向。 Now, it's reasonable to assume that the context vectors that are passed between the layers have some kind of meaning in embedding space -- given how people talk about them, I imagine some tests have been done to check, though perhaps that's a deep interpretability problem -- but the important thing is that what is passed between the layers has already gone through this normalisation. 现在，合理的假设是层与层之间传递的上下文向量在嵌入空间中有某种含义——考虑到人们谈论它们的方式，我想应该有人做过测试来验证，不过这也许是一个深层的可解释性问题——但关键在于，层之间传递的内容已经经过了这种归一化。 That is, if we assume that what is coming out of a single layer -- MHA, normalisation, and all of the other stuff we're going to cover in the next few posts -- is a meaningful context vector in embedding space, then the weights that we have inside the MHA layer itself -- our Wquery, Wkey, and Wvalue matrices -- will be trained so that the values that come out of that pure MHA part of the layer will not be in embedding space in and of themselves. They will instead be trained to output numbers that *will* be in embedding space, *after they have been normalised*. 也就是说，假设单层的输出——MHA、归一化，以及接下来几篇文章要介绍的所有其他东西——是嵌入空间中有意义的上下文向量，那么 MHA 层内部的权重——Wquery、Wkey 和 Wvalue 矩阵——就会被训练成：纯 MHA 部分输出的值本身不在嵌入空间中，而是在归一化*之后*输出会位于嵌入空间中的数字。 The model I'm forming here is that the normalisation is not so much a mechanical thing that we're doing to the numbers that flow through the network; it's more of a constraint on the kinds of values that can flow through at particular points, and during training, our network learns to shape the "unconstrained" parts -- the attention weights -- so that as a whole it does the desired task while working within those constraints. 我形成的模型是：归一化与其说是对网络中流过的数字进行机械处理，不如说是对特定位置允许流过的数值类型施加约束；在训练过程中，网络学习塑造那些“未受约束”的部分——注意力权重——使整体在这些约束下完成任务。 A work-in-progress metaphor I have for this is that it's kind of like a company where the interactions between teams are strongly codified, but teams can work pretty much independently so long as they present the required "API" to other teams. I've heard that AWS works kind of like this; the team that is responsible for -- say -- their email-sending service has a lot of freedom in *how* they work, so long as they provide an email service that operates in a particular way. 我目前想到的比喻是：这有点像一家公司，团队之间的交互被严格编码，但只要向其他团队提供规定的“API”，各团队就几乎可以独立工作。我听说 AWS 就有点像这样；比如负责邮件发送服务的团队，在*如何*工作上有很大自由，只要提供按特定方式运行的邮件服务即可。 Might need more work, but I'll see if it sticks :-) 可能还需要进一步打磨，不过先看看这个比喻能否成立 :-) ### Scale and shift 缩放与平移 Once we've done all of this and have our context vectors all nicely aligned with a mean of 0 and a variance of 1, there's one final step; we multiply them by a *scale* vector, then add on a *shift* vector. Each of these has a length equal to the embedding dimensions -- that is, the zeroth number in a given context vector is multiplied by the zeroth one in the *scale* vector, then has the zeroth in the *shift* vector added on. These vectors are trainable -- a given normalisation step will use the same ones for every context vector, but the actual values to use will be one of the parameters learned as part of the training. 完成这些步骤、让上下文向量的均值为 0、方差为 1 后，还有最后一步：将它们乘以一个*缩放*向量，再加上一个*平移*向量。这两个向量的长度都等于嵌入维度——也就是说，给定上下文向量中的第 0 个数字乘以*缩放*向量中的第 0 个数字，再加上*平移*向量中的第 0 个数字。这些向量是可训练的——一次归一化步骤会对每个上下文向量使用同一组向量，但具体数值会作为训练时学习到的参数之一。 That kind of feels like it's undoing some of the work we've done to normalise things! I also can't think of an obvious mapping for either of them in the audio metaphor I've been using so far. 这感觉有点像把我们为归一化所做的一些工作又撤销了！而且在一直使用的音频比喻中，我也想不出对它们有什么明显对应。 But at a stretch, perhaps the scale vector could be seen as some kind of equaliser step? What it's doing is is saying that after this normalisation step, we're going to increase how much the context vectors point in certain dimensions, and decrease it in others. Perhaps an engineering trick that just happens to work? That feels like a bit of a cop-out, though. 勉强要类比的话，也许可以把缩放向量看成均衡器步骤？它的作用是说：经过归一化之后，我们要增加上下文向量在某些维度上的指向程度，并降低在另一些维度上的指向程度。也许这只是一个碰巧有效的工程技巧？不过这样说感觉有点搪塞。 The shift vector is even harder to put into the audio metaphor. I was thinking that it might be to avoid issues with the activation function that comes up later (having set the mean to zero means that we might "throw away" a lot of information with an activation function that treats numbers less than zero as zero), but there's a linear layer before that, which could perfectly well handle that side of things. 平移向量更难放进音频比喻。我曾想，它可能是为了避免后面出现的激活函数带来的问题（均值设为零后，面对把小于零的数字都当成零的激活函数，我们可能会“丢掉”很多信息），但在那之前还有一个线性层，完全可以处理这方面的问题。 After discussion with Claude, I think that the best way to look at it is that having a mean of zero and a variance of one is not necessarily the best set of statistical properties for the context vectors to have. By setting all of them to those values, but then applying scale and shift, we give the model a way to learn what the most appropriate statistical properties for them to have actually are, and then to use that. 和 Claude 讨论后，我认为更好的理解方式是：均值为零、方差为一不一定是上下文向量最理想的统计属性。先把它们都设成这些值，再应用缩放和平移，就给了模型学习最合适统计属性的途径，并能使用学到的属性。 The important thing is that all of the context vectors coming in will have different variances and means, while the ones going out will have the same. So perhaps that still works in the terms of "getting all of the incoming signals to the same level" metaphor, albeit at a level of abstraction that might be becoming a bit too high... 重要的是，输入的所有上下文向量会有不同的方差和均值，而输出的向量会拥有相同的方差和均值。因此，用“把所有输入信号调到同一电平”的比喻来说也许仍然成立，只是抽象层次可能已经高得有点过头了…… It's still a little foggy in my mind, though. Perhaps something where just doing some experiments would help -- another one to add to my ever-growing list of things to try out later! 我脑中还是有点模糊。也许动手做些实验会有帮助——又多了一件要加入我日益增长的待办清单、以后再尝试的事情！ ### Wrapping up 总结 So, as a first draft of a mental model for this -- layer normalisation constrains the values coming out of a particular attention layer so that they have a mean of zero -- no "DC bias" -- and they are within a reasonably similar range -- line signal level -- so that we don't have issues with exploding or vanishing gradients. We then apply a scale vector and a shift vector, which means that they now have the same mean and variance, but not necessarily zero and one. 所以，作为目前的第一版心智模型：层归一化约束特定注意力层输出的值，使均值为零——没有“直流偏置”——并处于大致相近的范围——线路信号电平——从而避免梯度爆炸或消失。接着应用缩放向量和平移向量，于是它们拥有相同的均值和方差，但不一定是零和一。 That all seems pretty reasonable! I think we can wrap this one up here, and next time I'll move on to another part of the folding, spindling and mutilating that we do to the outputs of our simple multi-head attention modules in order to make the network trainable and able to do its job. 这看起来相当合理！这篇就到这里，下一次我会继续介绍：为了让网络可训练、能够完成任务，我们还要对简单多头注意力模块的输出做哪些“折叠、穿孔和肢解”。 [Here's a link to the next post in this series](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2025/08/llm-from-scratch-17-the-feed-forward-network). [这是本系列下一篇文章的链接](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2025/08/llm-from-scratch-17-the-feed-forward-network)。 * * * 1. I realised this isn't quite right while writing [the next post in the series](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2025/07/llm-from-scratch-17-the-feed-forward-network). [↩](#fnref-1) 在写[本系列下一篇文章](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2025/07/llm-from-scratch-17-the-feed-forward-network)时，我意识到这并不完全正确。 [↩](#fnref-1) 2. Raschka points out that there is an actually more common way of doing this that applies "Bessel's correction", where instead of taking the mean of the squared differences, you add them up and then divide by n−1, where n is the number of elements in the vector, instead of just dividing by n. PyTorch actually does that by default, but he has code to tell it not to. Obviously the difference between dividing by n or by n−1 becomes pretty minor as n gets big (like it is with the hundreds of embedding dimensions LLMs use) so it doesn't really change things much -- the code to not use it is for compatibility with the pre-generated GPT-2 weights that we load into the LLM later, which were trained without this correction. Raschka 指出，其实有一种更常见的做法会应用“贝塞尔校正”：不取平方差的平均值，而是先将它们相加，再除以 n−1；n 是向量中的元素数，而不是简单除以 n。PyTorch 默认确实如此，但他的代码会告诉它不要这样做。显然，n 很大时（就像 LLM 使用数百个嵌入维度时），除以 n 还是 n−1 的差异会很小，因此对结果影响不大——禁用校正是为了兼容稍后加载到 LLM 中的预生成 GPT-2 权重，那些权重是在未做此校正的情况下训练的。 One thing that I noticed while messing around a bit with this is that whether or not we apply the correction doesn't change the procedure we need to follow; if we calculate the variance without the correction and then divide by the square root of that, we will get something that has a variance of 1 if that second variance is also calculated without the correction. Likewise, if we do both calculations with the correction applied, we'll also get a variance of 1. If we mix and match then we'll get weird results, but that would be a silly thing to do anyway. [↩](#fnref-2) 我在随便摆弄时注意到：无论是否应用校正，都不会改变我们需要遵循的过程；如果无校正计算方差，再除以它的平方根，那么只要第二次计算方差时也不校正，结果方差就是 1。同样，如果两次计算都应用校正，也会得到方差 1。混用两种方式才会得到奇怪结果，但那本来就是愚蠢的做法。 [↩](#fnref-2) 3. When I ran this past ChatGPT as a pre-post review, it helpfully pointed out that squaring is differentiable, while the the absolute value is not at 0. This is a good point, because we need everything to be differentiable in order to do gradient descent. That said, it seems unlikely that that was the original reason when the concept was invented way back when, and of course ReLU is also not technically differentiable -- but there are workarounds. Worth noting, though. [↩](#fnref-3) 我让 ChatGPT 在发布前帮忙审阅时，它很有帮助地指出，平方是可微的，而绝对值在 0 处不可微。这一点很重要，因为梯度下降要求所有操作都可微。不过，概念在很久以前被发明时，平方不太可能就是最初原因；当然 ReLU 在技术上也不可微——但有变通办法。值得注意。 [↩](#fnref-3)
